doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Playing in Ornette Coleman's Skies of America rehearsal
summary: Jimmy sat in on a rehearsal as a trombonist, took the bassoon part and suggested recording in England.

venues.name: New York Conservatory of Modern Music

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I noticed that you had played with Ornette Coleman too?
Actually it was a very short experience, but a very broad one, and that was when he had received a Guggenheim Award and they were doing the “Skies of America.”
Oh, yeah, the big orchestral piece.

With a big orchestra. And so the contractor had contacted a friend of mine, a French horn player, Les Ellman, who was responsible for me playing shows and things like that. And also, my friend Frank Cuomo, who I went to school with at the New York Conservatory of Modern Music, in terms of copying, were also professional copyists and orchestrators and all of that. So in dealing with that beforehand, that’s when he had his place on Prince Street. And so what happened, for the rehearsal Les asked me to bring the horn because he wanted to make sure he had everybody covered. And so sure enough we passed the music out and everything. So that’s how I got to play with him, because one of the trombone players was late. And so I sat down and he was rehearsing, and he was trying to get the reed section to do something. But he was speaking on behalf of nuances and everything. And he would play it, and he would try to see if he could get them to interpret it as closely as possible to it, and it was a pleasurable job because they were all legit players, really, they weren’t all jazz. It was a mixture of jazz players. Like the trombone player played saxes too, a fine jazz musician. And anyway, the trombone player finally showed up and so he was sitting there and he said well what’s wrong? He said where’s my part? And I realized I had his part, and I said, oh, look here. Here’s his part here. And I said there’s a bassoon part and I’ll take the bassoon part. And so I spent that whole two hours, professional pay of a two hour rehearsal at a small second level, working with my level. And then at the same time, both Les and I had explained to him that under the circumstances he was having such a problem, we thought he’d go broke before he could ever get that recorded. So we suggested to him that, “Look go to England. The scale for every rehearsal and everything is cheaper.” And that’s where he recorded it. He recorded © Fillius Jazz Archive -38-

it in England. And I’ve still got the bassoon part. So that was actually my experience with him, which was a great experience to see him handle all this and deal with it. And then finally to get a copy of the recording and see how it came out. And how are you going to beat the BBC?
